saccharomyces-ferment.summary: Filtered yeast-fermentation liquid, best known as Pitera in SK-II essences, used to leave skin feeling hydrated, smooth and brighter-looking.

quick.overview:
Saccharomyces ferment is the cosmetic name for a filtered product of yeast fermentation, found in essences and serums. People use it for skin that feels hydrated and supple and looks smoother and more radiant. Its best-known form is Pitera in SK-II.

The chain is topical: a yeast-ferment essence is applied after cleansing, skin feels softer and more hydrated, and the surface looks smoother and brighter. The brand says the product grew from observations of sake brewery workers with smooth hands. Published human studies of the ingredient itself are very limited; one registered trial covered probiotic skincare more broadly.
quick.how: Used as an essence or lotion patted onto clean skin after cleansing and before serum and moisturiser, in twice-daily routines. It is usually layered with other K-beauty or J-beauty steps. Users generally describe changes in feel within days and in look over several weeks of consistent use.
quick.risks: Used topically in cosmetics, with the usual chance of irritation or sensitivity for some skin. SK-II products were involved in 2005-2006 complaints and temporary sales suspensions in China and South Korea, after which regulators reported trace elements were unlikely to harm health.

angle.text: Yeast ferment filtrate, best known from SK-II's Pitera, is applied as an essence to leave skin feeling hydrated and supple, which reads as smoother, more radiant skin. Users of K-beauty essences layer it into daily routines for that glow.

kombucha-ferment.summary: Tea or plant extract fermented with a kombucha culture, used in serums and toners as an antioxidant, calming ingredient for fresher-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Kombucha ferment is made by fermenting tea or botanical extracts with a kombucha culture of bacteria and yeast. It appears in serums and toners, where people use it for fresher, brighter, calmer-looking skin.

The chain is antioxidant: the fermentation converts sugars into organic acids and alters the extract's polyphenols, and lab studies report higher antioxidant activity in some fermented extracts. The idea is less oxidative stress on skin and a healthier-looking complexion. Published work so far consists of laboratory studies on cells and chemical assays; human skincare trials were not found.
quick.how: Applied as a toner, essence or serum after cleansing, usually in a morning and evening routine alongside a moisturiser and sunscreen. It tends to be one of several botanical steps in a K-beauty-style routine. Users describe the effect as a gradual change in freshness over a few weeks.
quick.risks: Topical safety data were not found. Reports of serious adverse events relate mainly to drinking home-brewed kombucha rather than skincare. As with any new topical, a patch test on a small area is the usual precaution for reactive skin.

angle.text: Kombucha ferment goes into serums and toners as an antioxidant, calming botanical aimed at fresher, brighter-looking skin. Lab studies on fermented extracts report higher antioxidant activity, which is the route to less oxidative stress on the skin surface.

tremella-mushroom.summary: Snow fungus polysaccharide used in Asian skincare as a plant-based hydrator for plumper, smoother-looking skin and softer fine lines.

quick.overview:
Tremella, or snow fungus, is an edible gelatinous fungus whose polysaccharide extracts are used in Asian skincare as a plant alternative to hyaluronic acid. People use it for skin that stays hydrated, looks plumper and shows softer fine lines.

The chain is water-holding: its polysaccharides are described as absorbing and holding water at the skin surface, so skin feels and looks more hydrated. A patent also reports inhibition of melanin formation, which is why some products pitch it for brightening. The sources found are encyclopedic descriptions and patents; clinical trials were not found.
quick.how: Used in essences, serums, creams and masks, applied to clean skin as a hydrating step under moisturiser. It is often combined with other humectants such as hyaluronic acid or glycerin. Users commonly report skin feeling more hydrated right after application, with a more lasting effect from consistent daily use.
quick.risks: No skincare safety data were found. The fungus itself is a long-established food in Chinese cuisine, and topical products carry standard irritation precautions.

angle.text: Tremella polysaccharides are used in Asian skincare as a plant-based alternative to hyaluronic acid, holding water at the skin surface so skin looks plumper and fine lines look softer. A patent also describes it reducing melanin formation for a brighter tone.

mugwort.summary: Artemisia herb used in K-beauty toners and masks to calm redness and give reactive skin a more even look; pollen allergy is common.

quick.overview:
Mugwort is a name for several Artemisia species long used in food, folk medicine and moxibustion, and now a staple of K-beauty toners and masks. People with reactive skin use it for a calmer, less red, more even-looking complexion.

The chain is soothing: extracts contain terpenes such as cineole, camphor and thujone, which preliminary studies associate with antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity, and the idea is less visible irritation and redness. Its folk use is long; human trials of mugwort skincare were not found.
quick.how: Applied as a toner, essence, sheet mask or cream after cleansing, often in routines built for sensitive or redness-prone skin. It is usually combined with other calming ingredients such as centella or panthenol. Users generally describe calmer skin within days to a few weeks.
quick.risks: Mugwort pollen is a common allergen, and the plant may trigger reactions in people sensitive to the daisy family (Asteraceae). Thujone is a neurotoxin at high concentrations, and herbal safety guidance advises against use in pregnancy. A patch test is the usual precaution.

angle.text: Mugwort extract is used in K-beauty toners and masks by people with reactive skin who want a calmer, less red complexion. Its terpenes show anti-inflammatory activity in preliminary studies, which is the route to less visible irritation.

houttuynia-cordata.summary: Fish mint (heartleaf) extract in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks, used to calm redness and keep oily, blemish-prone skin looking clearer.

quick.overview:
Houttuynia cordata, called fish mint or heartleaf, is a herb eaten in East and Southeast Asia and used in traditional medicine. Its extract is common in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks used for calming redness and oily, blemish-prone skin.

The chain is soothing: flavonoids such as quercitrin lower inflammatory mediators and show antioxidant effects in cell studies, and extracts have antibacterial activity against acne bacteria in vitro. The result people want is less visible irritation and blemishing and a clearer, calmer look. Support comes mainly from cell studies and a small reported toner study; controlled skin trials were not found.
quick.how: Applied as a toner, serum or sheet mask after cleansing, often as the calming step in routines for oily or breakout-prone skin. It is commonly paired with centella, salicylic acid or niacinamide products. Users typically report calmer skin within days to weeks.
quick.risks: Contact dermatitis is reported in sensitive users, and a patch test is the usual advice. Injectable forms have caused severe allergic reactions, and high oral doses were toxic in animal studies.

angle.text: Heartleaf extract is used in Korean toners, serums and sheet masks to calm redness and keep oily, blemish-prone skin looking clearer. Its flavonoids lower inflammatory signals and act against acne bacteria in cell studies, which is the route to less visible irritation.

ginseng-root-extract.summary: Korean-herb root extract used in K-beauty and herbal skincare as an antioxidant for healthier, more youthful-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Ginseng root extract comes from Panax ginseng, a root central to East Asian traditional medicine. In skincare it shows up in K-beauty and herbal products, used for a fresher, healthier, more youthful look.

The chain proponents describe is antioxidant: ginsenosides in the root reduced inflammatory and oxidative signalling in cell and animal studies, which maps to less oxidative stress in skin. Most published research is on oral ginseng for general health, where systematic reviews found efficacy could not be established; no clinical trial of topical use for appearance was found.
quick.how: Used in creams, essences, serums and herbal soaps as an antioxidant or soothing botanical, usually within a wider anti-aging routine with sunscreen and moisturiser. Some people also take it orally as a supplement. Users describe cumulative, gradual changes over weeks of use.
quick.risks: Oral ginseng has reported side effects, including headache, insomnia and raised blood pressure, and interacts with drugs such as warfarin. Topical products carry standard external-use and irritation warnings.

angle.text: Ginseng root extract is used in K-beauty and herbal skincare as an antioxidant that gives skin a healthier, more youthful look. Ginsenosides lowered oxidative and inflammatory signalling in cell and animal studies, and the research on ginseng is mostly about oral use.

portulaca-oleracea.summary: Purslane extract in soothing essences and moisturisers, used to calm irritated skin and leave it looking smoother and less red.

quick.overview:
Purslane is a common edible succulent used in folk medicine in many countries, and its extract now appears in K-beauty-style soothing essences and moisturisers. People use it to calm irritated skin so it looks less red and feels smoother and more hydrated.

The chain is soothing: flavonoids, alkaloids and fatty acids in the plant show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory assays, and a mouse study reported faster excision-wound closure with a crude topical preparation. Controlled clinical trials of topical purslane for appearance were not found.
quick.how: Applied as an essence, cream or mask after cleansing, often combined with other calming or hydrating ingredients such as niacinamide, glycerin or lotus extract. It is typically a daily step in routines for stressed or reactive skin, with changes described over days to weeks.
quick.risks: Leaves are high in oxalates when eaten. Topical product labels advise avoiding broken skin and stopping use if irritation occurs.

angle.text: Purslane extract appears in soothing essences and moisturisers that people use to calm irritated skin and reduce redness. Lab assays show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity, and a mouse study reported faster wound closure, which is the route to calmer, smoother skin.

scutellaria-baicalensis-root-extract.summary: Baikal skullcap root extract used in cosmetics as an anti-inflammatory and brightening botanical for redness and uneven tone.

quick.overview:
Baikal skullcap root (huangqin) is one of the fundamental herbs of traditional Chinese medicine, and its extract is used in some cosmetics aimed at redness and uneven skin tone. People use it for calmer, brighter-looking skin.

The chain is anti-inflammatory and antioxidant: flavonoids such as baicalin, baicalein and wogonin showed these activities in cell and animal studies, pointing to less inflammation and less pigment. A 2025 safety assessment reviewed it as a cosmetic ingredient, and two small registered trials have tested creams for hyperpigmentation, though results were not located.
quick.how: Applied in creams, serums and brightening or calming products as part of a daily routine, usually alongside sunscreen since tone work depends on sun protection. Users typically look for changes in tone over several weeks.
quick.risks: A case report describes allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic containing it, and oral supplements have been linked to liver injury in case reports. A patch test is the usual precaution for topical use.

angle.text: Baikal skullcap root extract is used in cosmetics as an anti-inflammatory and brightening botanical, aimed at redness and uneven tone. Its flavonoids, including baicalin and wogonin, show antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cell studies, and two small hyperpigmentation cream trials are registered.

perilla-seed-extract.summary: Seed extract from an Asian culinary herb, used in cosmetics as a plant omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient for softer, healthier-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Perilla seed extract comes from Perilla frutescens, a mint-family herb used in Korean, Chinese, Japanese and Indian cooking; the seeds are roughly 38 to 45 percent oil. It appears in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, used for softer, smoother, more comfortable skin.

The chain is barrier support: the plant oils soften the skin surface, and the extract and its component luteolin reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies. Published work is limited to laboratory and animal studies; human appearance trials were not found.
quick.how: Used in creams, oils and serums as a botanical emollient step after cleansing, often layered with other moisturising ingredients. Users typically describe softer skin soon after application and a gradual improvement in comfort and smoothness over weeks.
quick.risks: Perilla seed allergy, including anaphylaxis, is documented in children and adults, and contact dermatitis can occur from handling. People with seed allergies commonly avoid it.

angle.text: Perilla seed extract is included in some cosmetics as a plant-based omega-3 and antioxidant ingredient, used for softer, smoother skin. The oil-rich seed softens the skin surface, and the extract reduced inflammatory signalling in animal and cell studies.

camellia-japonica-extract.summary: Japanese camellia botanical used in some cosmetics for anti-aging, brightening and soothing, backed by a mouse study and Korean patent filings.

quick.overview:
Camellia japonica extract comes from the Japanese camellia, a flowering evergreen whose leaves contain anti-inflammatory terpenoids such as lupeol and squalene. It is used in some cosmetics, and Korean patent filings from 2004 and 2005 describe it for anti-aging, whitening and anti-inflammatory purposes.

The chain people are after is less inflammation and less pigment, giving brighter, younger-looking skin. The published research is a 2025 study in hairless mice, in which topical extract reduced atopic-dermatitis-like signs. Human studies were not found.
quick.how: Found in creams and serums as a botanical ingredient within anti-aging or brightening routines, usually used alongside sunscreen and a moisturiser. Users typically expect gradual changes over weeks.
quick.risks: No safety data for human cosmetic use were found. As with any new botanical, a patch test is the usual precaution.

angle.text: Japanese camellia extract is used in some cosmetics, with Korean patents describing it for anti-aging, brightening and soothing skin. Its terpenoids are anti-inflammatory, and a 2025 mouse study reported reduced skin inflammation signs.

hemp-seed-oil.summary: Linoleic-rich plant oil used in moisturisers, soaps and haircare to leave skin soft, smooth and well hydrated.

quick.overview:
Hemp seed oil is pressed from the seeds of low-THC hemp plants and is high in linoleic and alpha-linolenic fatty acids. It appears in moisturisers, soaps and haircare, used by people who want soft, smooth, well-hydrated skin.

The chain is emollient: the fatty-rich oil sits on the skin surface, supports the barrier and seals in moisture. Proponents attribute benefits to its essential fatty acids, which is described mainly in product labelling and composition studies. Two small registered human studies of topical hemp oil products exist; results were not found. It is distinct from CBD extracts.
quick.how: Used as a face or body oil, or in creams, applied after cleansing or on damp skin to lock in moisture, and in hair products as a conditioning oil. It is often layered over a humectant such as hyaluronic acid or glycerin. Users generally notice softness right away.
quick.risks: Topical products carry standard external-use labelling. Analytical studies have measured trace cannabinoids in some commercial oils, carried over from plant material during processing. Patch testing is the usual precaution for sensitive skin.

angle.text: Hemp seed oil is used in moisturisers and body care by people wanting soft, well-hydrated skin. Its high linoleic acid content helps support the skin barrier and seal in moisture, leaving skin looking smoother.

volcanic-ash.summary: Fine volcanic rock used in some K-beauty masks and cleansers to absorb surface oil and leave oily skin looking matte and clearer.

quick.overview:
Ground volcanic ash and related volcanic minerals appear in some Korean-origin masks and cleansers as oil-absorbing ingredients. People with oily skin use them for less shine, cleaner-feeling pores and a matte, clearer look.

The chain is absorption: the fine mineral particles take up surface sebum, so skin looks less shiny and pores look less clogged. Users and marketing describe this effect; no study of cosmetic volcanic ash on human skin was identified, and the literature found covers volcanology and exposure hazards.
quick.how: Used as a wash-off mask or cleanser, typically applied to the oily zones for several minutes once or twice a week, then rinsed and followed by moisturiser. It is often combined with other clay or charcoal products. Matte results are visible right after rinsing.
quick.risks: Raw eruption ash is abrasive and can irritate eyes, skin and airways. Cosmetic safety data were not found, and drying or over-cleansing can irritate skin.

angle.text: Volcanic ash appears in some K-beauty masks and cleansers, used to absorb oil and leave oily skin looking matte. The fine mineral particles take up surface sebum, which means less shine and cleaner-looking pores.

witch-hazel-extract.summary: Classic astringent toner botanical used to reduce shine and give oily or blemish-prone skin a tighter feel and smaller-looking pores.

quick.overview:
Witch hazel extract comes from the bark and leaves of a North American shrub and is the classic astringent toner. People with oily or blemish-prone skin use it to reduce shine and get a tighter feel with smaller-looking pores.

The chain is astringent: it is rich in tannins such as hamamelitannin, which tighten the skin surface and reduce oil feel. Native American and later settler use on swellings and external inflammations is part of its history. Published literature is laboratory work, including antibacterial studies of a standardised extract; human trials of its toner effect were not identified.
quick.how: Applied with a cotton pad or sprayed after cleansing, usually once or twice daily on oily areas, before serum and moisturiser. It is often combined with other oil-control steps. The tightening feel is immediate.
quick.risks: Traditional toner distillates are made with alcohol, which can dry or sting sensitive skin. Safety data were not reviewed in the available sources, and alcohol-free versions exist.

angle.text: Witch hazel is a classic astringent toner used by people with oily or blemish-prone skin to cut shine and get a tighter feel. Its tannins act on the skin surface, which reads as less oil and smaller-looking pores.

pine-bark-extract.summary: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol), a procyanidin antioxidant taken or applied in anti-aging and skin-brightening routines.

quick.overview:
Maritime pine bark extract is a proanthocyanidin-rich supplement made from the bark of Pinus pinaster, best known under the trademark Pycnogenol, which contains 70% procyanidins. People take or apply it as an antioxidant in anti-aging and skin-brightening routines, aiming for firmer, more even-looking skin.

The chain is antioxidant: laboratory work reports antioxidant activity and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes linked to collagen breakdown. Human trials have looked at blood pressure, ADHD, asthma, venous insufficiency and osteoarthritis, and a Cochrane review updated in 2020 found insufficient evidence across those conditions. Skin-appearance trials were not found.
quick.how: Taken as a daily oral capsule, or used in some skincare products. People often combine it with other antioxidant supplements and sunscreen in anti-aging routines, and describe changes over a period of weeks to months.
quick.risks: Detailed safety information was not available in the reviewed sources. As with any supplement, people on medication or who are pregnant commonly check with a clinician first.

angle.text: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol) is taken or applied as an antioxidant in anti-aging and skin-brightening routines, aiming at firmer, more even-looking skin. Lab work shows antioxidant activity and inhibition of collagen-degrading enzymes, while human trials have studied conditions such as blood pressure and ADHD.

mistletoe-extract.summary: Mistletoe botanical used in some Korean-style skincare for soothing and general skin health; its human research is in cancer care.

quick.overview:
Mistletoe extract comes from European mistletoe (Viscum album). It appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare products, where it is used for soothing and a healthier-looking complexion.

The chain claimed is soothing and antioxidant action on the skin. Mistletoe's published human research is in cancer care: injectable extracts such as Iscador have been used as complementary treatments, and mistletoe lectins have been reported to stimulate immune signalling. No study of mistletoe on skin or appearance was identified.
quick.how: In skincare it is used as one botanical among others in creams, serums and essences within a daily routine. Medicinal injectable extracts are a separate use, administered in clinical settings.
quick.risks: The plant contains the toxin viscumin, which works by a mechanism similar to ricin; European mistletoe is described as more toxic than American mistletoe. Topical cosmetic safety was not covered in the reviewed sources, and the plant is not meant to be eaten.

angle.text: Mistletoe extract appears as a botanical in some Korean-style skincare, used for soothing and healthier-looking skin. Its published research is in complementary cancer care, with immune-signalling effects reported for its lectins.

noni-fruit-extract.summary: Pacific fruit extract sold as juice, supplements and cosmetics as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion.

quick.overview:
Noni is a tropical fruit spread across the Pacific by Polynesian sailors, used traditionally as a tonic and now sold as juice, supplements and in cosmetics. People use it as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion.

The chain is antioxidant: the fruit contains anthraquinones, iridoids, flavonoids and scopoletin, and an anthraquinone from noni was reported to boost extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured human skin fibroblasts. That is cell-culture work; Wikipedia states there is no confirmed clinical efficacy for any use, and no skin-appearance trial was identified.
quick.how: Taken as a juice or supplement, or applied in creams and serums, usually as part of a wider anti-aging routine. Users describe gradual changes over weeks.
quick.risks: Anthraquinones can be harmful, and a 2024 review is cited as linking oral noni products to liver disease risk. The FDA issued a 2018 warning letter to a noni marketer over unapproved drug claims. People with liver conditions commonly avoid oral noni.

angle.text: Noni extract is sold as juice, supplements and cosmetics as an antioxidant for a brighter, more youthful complexion. An anthraquinone from the fruit boosted extracellular matrix synthesis in cultured skin cells, which is the route to firmer-looking skin.

moringa.summary: Tropical tree whose seed oil and leaf extract are used in skin and hair products as a light moisturiser and antioxidant for smoother skin.

quick.overview:
Moringa oleifera is a fast-growing tropical tree, and its seed oil (ben oil) and leaf extracts appear in creams, body oils and hair products. People use them as a light moisturiser and antioxidant for smoother, healthier-looking skin.

The chain has two parts: the fatty-acid-rich oil acts as an emollient that softens and protects the skin surface, and phenolic compounds such as quercetin and kaempferol show antioxidant activity in laboratory studies of leaf extracts. No human trial found tests moringa for skin appearance.
quick.how: Used as a body or face oil, in creams, or in hair products, applied after cleansing or to damp skin to seal in moisture. Users notice softness soon after application and describe smoother skin with regular use over weeks.
quick.risks: Topical products are generally labelled for external use. Oral use has limited human toxicity data and possible drug-metabolism interactions per Wikipedia, and Australia and New Zealand declined novel-food approval in 2025.

angle.text: Moringa seed oil and leaf extract are used in skin and hair products as a light moisturiser and antioxidant for smoother, healthier-looking skin. The oil softens and protects the skin surface, and leaf extracts show antioxidant activity in laboratory studies.

yuzu-extract.summary: Citrus extract used in Asian skincare as a vitamin C and polyphenol botanical for brighter, more even skin tone.

quick.overview:
Yuzu is a tart citrus fruit grown mainly in Japan and Korea, and extracts of its peel, juice or seed appear in some Asian skin-care products for their vitamin C and polyphenol content. People use it for brighter, more even skin tone.

The chain is antioxidant and pigment: in cell studies a yuzu seed compound, nomilin, showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cultured melanoma cells, pointing to less pigment and a more even tone. Published work is laboratory and animal studies; human skin trials were not found.
quick.how: Used in serums, creams, masks and toners as a brightening step, typically in a morning and evening routine paired with sunscreen, which tone-evening depends on. Users generally look for changes over several weeks.
quick.risks: No specific safety data for cosmetic use were found; citrus ingredients can irritate or sensitise some skin. A patch test is the usual precaution.

angle.text: Yuzu extract is used in Asian skincare as a vitamin C and polyphenol botanical for brighter, more even skin tone. A yuzu seed compound showed antioxidant activity and lowered melanin production in cell studies, which is the route to less pigment.

horse-oil.summary: Emollient fat (ma-yu) used in Japanese and Korean creams to seal in moisture and leave skin softer and smoother.

quick.overview:
Horse oil (ma-yu) is a fat rendered from horse tissue and used as an emollient in skin-care creams, particularly in Japan and Korea. People use it for rich moisture and softer, smoother-looking skin.

The chain is skin-like lipids: its fatty acids, including linoleic and palmitoleic acids, have been described as similar to human skin lipids, so it seals moisture into the skin. Small formulation and laboratory studies, including Korean work on microneedle patches and cultured skin cells, report barrier-supporting and antioxidant effects. Independent clinical trials in people were not found.
quick.how: Applied as a cream, balm or oil, typically as the last step of a routine to seal in moisture, and common on dry areas. Users notice softness soon after application.
quick.risks: No safety data specific to people were found in the sources reviewed. It is an animal-derived product, which some people avoid, and researchers have studied methods for detecting adulterated oil.

angle.text: Horse oil (ma-yu) is used in Japanese and Korean creams as a rich emollient, chosen because its fatty acids resemble human skin lipids. It seals moisture into the skin for a softer, smoother look, with small formulation and cell studies reporting barrier support.

starfish-extract.summary: K-beauty marine ingredient inspired by starfish regrowing arms, used for moisturising and a smoother, younger-looking skin.

quick.overview:
Starfish extract is a preparation from sea star tissues, listed in some Korean beauty products as a moisturising or regenerating ingredient. It draws on the starfish's ability to regrow lost arms, and people use it for smoother, younger-looking skin.

The chain claimed is repair and hydration. The published evidence is a 2016 zebrafish study and a few patents, plus a study in which fractions from regenerating starfish tissue boosted cell proliferation and migration in wound-healing assays. Human trials were not found.
quick.how: Used in creams, serums and masks within anti-aging and hydrating routines, applied after cleansing and under moisturiser. Users describe changes as gradual, over weeks.
quick.risks: No human safety data were found. Wikipedia notes that some starfish contain saponins and, in certain species, toxins, though cosmetic extracts were not addressed.

angle.text: Starfish extract is a K-beauty marine ingredient used for moisturising and regenerating skin, inspired by starfish regrowing lost arms. A study of regenerating starfish tissue reported boosted cell proliferation and migration in wound-healing assays, and the line from there to smoother, younger-looking skin is the claim.
